items.text: I agree with Misti Y-- that some people may love the cirque shows and still dislike Le Reve. But that is really a separate discussion. For me the theater and visual design are the best parts. The scenery and decor are breathtaking start to end. The whole concept of the show is really beautiful and appealing. Unfortunately it doesn't translate very well to live performance. The storyline isn't very entertaining at all. When I attended a performance the stage malfunctioned repeatedly through the night. It was really difficult to be entertained. And during some of the more impressive scenes it was really hard to stay engaged. Le Reve is trying to reach for some of that flare and spectacle that cirque is associated with, but it doesn't get there. I would mostly go if it was the chance to experience that beautiful theater. But otherwise you're probably better off spending your money on another show.

38 dollars. i think i got my 38 dollars worth, maybe a little more. i think i should have asked the seller what switches it used before i bought it, but i got tired of waiting, so just bought it. i asked in a message, and got my answer a week after i already had it on my desk. Brown switches, just saying.
the space bar rattle. i get used to it through the day, but after 23-24, i type around it. "E" just re-peats, not every time, like in a few paragraphs once. I read all over before hit send because sometimes "meeting" becomes "meeeting", I have to check.
But for comfort, I would keep it. It has a bump on every key, part of the way down. So I can press it, and my finger can know that I've registered the press, without slamming it. So I can type a long mail and my wrists don't hurt, which I can't do with the flat laptop keys.
Now I was thinking of sending it back, but the return shipping is gonna eat up half of the cost. And I would have to go back to typing on my laptop, so I'm keeping it with rattle all.

So I just saw this theatrical circus style show in Vegas and I recommend it, just deducting one star. The story line can be a little hard to follow and some of the songs seem sleepy, wrong for the action. But the performers are just amazing, great athletic abilities, bodies, and aerobic abilities. And the female performers in particular were very impressive, they stay underwater for minutes at a time. The theatre is round, the stage is round, so all seats get a good view. There are 3 major stage entrances that are used throughout the show, which becomes very important in major story line turns. The stage and general setting and lighting is beautiful and makes a memorable atmosphere. Ticket prices were also reasonable compared to other big Vegas shows like O or Love. Wished it had more cool special effects. More fire, but this is not a big problem. With the story line and music problems, it is still a fun, visually beautiful show that I recommend.

There's a lot of people saying remote work is a panacea. But you know from my two years of mentoring 5 junior engineers, it really is overblown for any juniors still learning how to code. They don't need tickets, or documentation or meetings. They need to sit in on design conversations. They need to see how others debug issues. They need to ask questions before they have hours of confusion. That kind of interaction happens organically in an office. For remote work, they need to know the right times to cut in, set up a call, and explain a problem that they might not even fully understand yet, so it's a skill and a tough one! To have it, before you have a chance to learn it. I've seen the feedback issues in remote work. Short comments on code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. Also, it takes longer, so you have less momentum. The jrs I mentored typically improved faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. and had easy access to seniors. I'm not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for jrs, proximity is a booster, for confidence, context, and instincts. And sending jrs off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development which can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

So, the mixer was just going, that low drone that vibrates up through your boots and all, flour dust just floating in the air and catching the bad fluorescent light, like snow suspended. 3:17 AM. The sourdough was resting on wooden boards, still kind of soft with pale crusts, waiting for the final bake. Elias wiped his hands on his apron, stiff as board with all the dried dough and sweat. He walked to the front counter to check the lock, just one of those paranoia things, not like you really need to do it every night.

And there it sat. The History of Salt. Hardback, spine was blue and it was cracked near the hinge. The book had shown up every Thursday for six weeks, always on the glass display case beside the cinnamon rolls and it wasn't sold. There was no library stamp saying it belonged to the city system, because it wasn't a branch, not the municipal library, so the bakery got it. So he picked it up. It was cold to the touch. Opened it and expected blank pages or maybe some forgotten bookmark. But a folded square of lined paper just fell out and landed on the counter with a soft tap.

He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, really pressed hard into the fiber of the paper. What it said was: you knead with your left hand dominant, stop favoring the right, it ruins the tension. So Elias stared at that, then looked at his own hands, red knuckled, white with dust. The mixer ticked into the next cycle. He closed the book, aligned the spine back on the glass display case, perfect. Then he turned off the overhead light and just left it there in shadow.

Apple does deserve a mention. It comes from what happened to me. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high school and even though they cost about twice as much as PC ones. They broke every month or so. The hard drive went on my laptop, I replaced it five times over four years. I never once dropped it but had to reinstall the OS a few times, and on one occasion it actually did. Worst part is, apple support never really fixed it, every single time they just backed up, wiped, restored. A friend of mine got a MacBook Pro on fire once while watching a movie. Smoke alarm went off. Also my iPhone, which was the first model, misbehaved a lot. But now I think Apple just releases a new iPhone every two months or so, and it has like a bit better camera and that's it. One good thing and its iPad which is still probably the best tablet out there, but android may very well catch up.

Saw Awakening at Wynn Las Vegas. Fine, but not the Vegas must-see I’d build a trip around. Las Vegas has been my playground since childhood, so I’ve seen a ton of shows before 21, decent baseline. The circular stage is genuinely smart, every seat gets a decent view, rare in big shows. Wynn or Encore guests get a deal, $125 tickets become $99, that helps. Some individual acts are impressive, performers are clearly strong as hell. Aerialists, acrobats, stuff. Lot of feats feel just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. But story is the problem. Unclear, weak, or no story, I left not knowing what it was trying to say. Too much going on, too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many attempts to be “wow.” More restrained would hit harder. Aside from a few cool stunts, average. Not blown away. No one I was with seemed overwhelmed. A few friends did enjoy, so check it out if you’ve never seen it, especially Wynn/Encore deal. But wouldn’t see again or pay full price a second time. Tries to be stereotypical huge flashy spectacle where more equals better. More just meant messier for me.

I got this mechanical keyboard used for $38, and it's been a mess but actually decent. The seller was terrible. I messaged them on the switch type before I bought it, took a full week to reply one word, so I just gambled on it. The board is heavily used, "well-loved" maybe. The spacebar has a really annoying rattle sounds like a loose Lego brick. The E key will repeat and double type so i get typos theee instead of the, which is kinda funny. But here's the thing, despite all these weird things, I actually really like to type on it. The tactile feedback is good, and its really comfortable for long work emails. I even considered returning it but it's a slab of plastic that weighs a lot and its more hassle than $38 is worth. I just kept it and I even really grown fond of the flaws. But if you don't mind some diy tuning and a double typing letter, its a budget win.

it works by having a buoyant float hooked to a valve. If the water drops, the float sinks, valve opens, water in. As it fills the float rises, shuts the valve off. At the set level, filling stops. Two things can make it overflow, not just close but overflow, and that is debris or mineral buildup on the valve stopping it from shutting fully, or that set level is too high from bad float adjustment.

Its a tough time, I know. The problems we are dealing with internally, and on top of what's going on in the world, doesnt feel much like a holiday season.

We had much discussion about whether to proceed with the all Enron holiday party scheduled Dec. 8. People felt different ways. Some felt it would be a good opportunity for us to get together, some felt it was inappropriate. I get both.

So basically, if you want to understand a siphon, its just an application of gravity and atmospheric pressure. I have been seeing too much of it online but I think its very neat as a process. To move the liquid over an elevated barrier, you have to fill the tube to get the full column of liquid. The water is pulled by gravity over the lip and the outlet must be lower than the source water surface. If the outlet is lower, the weight difference of water column in both legs is what powers the whole system. It will keep flowing over the hump. If the outlet is even level with source or higher, the gravitational force will be insufficient to lift water up. The net gravitational pull will only exist if the column of water exiting is heavier than the column of water rising, so it makes sense. The air bubbles are bad. If air enters the tube the continuous liquid column is broken. It messes up the cohesive chain of water molecules that lets it transmit the suction. Pressure inside the tube gets equalized to the outside atmosphere, then pressure differential stops so flow stops. And the siphon is failed, needs to re-prime it and fill it up entirely with liquid to get back.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. Again. Every Thursday this happens, it's always sitting right on top of the flour bin and there's always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing it, but honestly at 3am I'm running on pure yeast and caffeine anyway so maybe not that surprising. Only tonight something new, there was a scrap of yellow legal paper stuck to the book as though it was a bookmark. Wiped my hands on my apron leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth and pulled it out. It read page 142, please. I think they're watching the drop box now. Frantic spiky handwriting. I looked out to the darkened front windows and got nothing but my own tired reflection staring back at me, and there was a cold draft blowing through the kitchen smelling of wet asphalt and rain about to hit. I didn't open the book, just put the note back between the pages carefully. Then I slid the book into a brown pastry bag and folded the top twice to seal it.

Picked up a used mechanical for $38. I mean, you got $38 worth of keyboard. Maybe a tad more.

Look, it is not without its issues. Spacebar has a real rattle. It sounds like a tray of cutlery getting nudged, loose clatter every time my thumb slams it. I don't register it during the day, but at night when its loud, it's louder than it should be. Also the E key will repeat on me. I type meeting and it comes out meeeting. Happens once every few paragraphs, not constantly but often enough to keep me proofing. Seller took a whole week to reply to my initial question about switches which was after it arrived, brown switches.

That is all I can complain about really, other than it's just comfortable. Keys feel cushioned. I can type long stuff for hours without my wrists doing complaints on me. My laptop keyboard I used before I was using is flatter, this is more of a cushioned feel.

I thought about returning it, but was not worth the hassle. It sits on my desk and I just live with it. It is a little rattle, and a little repeat, and it earns its keep quietly.

3 stars

And the type of brother who is loyal and generous, the kind that will travel completely unreasonable distances to save you from your own stupidity. So Tom, we're really happy that you've found someone that loves you like we do, and unlike me, decided to room with you on a voluntary basis.

I rate this show 4 stars as a neutral view but its only a 2.5 to me. I have never wanted to see Cirque du Soleil before and this was the first, called Le Reve. I was expecting to see lots of backflips, extreme acrobatics but I actually saw less of this than I expected and I saw mostly interpretive dancing. The talent of performers was very impressive no doubt about it but it is not my style. For this kind of show, if you enjoy theatrical spectacle for real then you'll probably enjoy this. But as a personal preference I wouldn't pay more than $100 to go to this kind of show. Luckily I went on free tickets so I didn't pay.

Old school attendance registers have been really useful for historical studies, helping reconstruct things about past life patterns, which are missing from official stories. It shows which children attended, how regular they were, and in some cases why they weren't present. It allows historians to make inferences on seasonal work demands, illness, bad weather, poverty, care for family, migration, or local emergencies. It might show differences across gender, age, neighbourhood, and social class. So it helps us understand the position of education in work and household routine and expectations of the community. When looked at over years, it shows change in habits of schooling and changes in public health. But a limitation is that the registers record only what the school chose to record, and they won't explain childrens' experiences. There's a chance absences are misreported, or incomplete, or based on assumption of teachers. So it's not a good source alone. But when combined with other sources, it does provide insights to reconstruct history.

Mara was doing some croissants, pressing the butter into the dough, and the latch goes this tiny almost guilty click. There’s nobody there. The book is just sitting dry as a bone on the wet concrete.
She was wiping her hands on her apron when she opened it. A slip of paper, folded once, between Luna moth and promethea. “Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs”. She looked out at the alley, the dented milk crates, the steam coming off the drains, and for a second the city felt enormous, then it didn’t. She tore off a corner of the order pad and wrote “Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05”. Then she put the note in the book and put the book on the warm windowsill and she unlocked the back door.

We compared the stability of folded cardboard bridge designs. So simple stuff, controlled testing. The students built short beam, arch inspired, and triangular fold bridges from the same cardboard. Tries to keep length and width consistent each time, but by hand its hard to do, so not always the same. Each bridge went between two supports and added weights. Gradually, watching the bridge bend, tip over or collapse. So its limited. Its hand made, small number of trials, and classroom testing. So we dont take the results like engineering data. But what seems to be. The triangular fold seemed to be more stable holding the weight. So the fold does affect stability in model bridges.

She found it on the steel table behind the back door. Under the bench by where the bread peels hang. Coastal birds field guide. There was a Harbor Street branch stamp in it and March due date. Old story, actually, that door mail slot had been nailed up for years but the hatch is the old flour man hatch and it doesn't close properly, never really latches. So she figured, eleven Thursday books and she had asked day staff to check the hatch for scratches. She also stayed till four with her coat on once, waiting to see it. But it always turned up between two and four. And I'm at the ovens most of the time. Back to the door. Never see it.
Tonight one of the grocery receipts from Pell's was folded in the book. Oystercatchers pages. Handwriting in it. Ink all blotchy where someone pressed hard. *I keep meaning to take this back to library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.* Whoever it was she thought. Book smelled of salt.
She pulled a pencil from her apron and on the back of the receipt she wrote. *Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll.* Then tucked it back in the oystercatchers. Set book on the hatch ledge. Warm roll in a paper bag next to it.

i moved to Toronto so im off the hydro ottawa system but i want people to know what they got up to. i had an account for a year when i was renting downtown. when i went back to my parents for my MA, i closed it out for sure and paid every last charge that was due. but just because its closed does not mean they stop just because its closed they still took payment from my other bank account. and it was at random times, it would go for months. i called the customer service a couple of times sent them proof of the withdrawal of payment. they just said its closed, no debit occurring. it was only once me and my parents cross checked our bills, we found out it was linked my bank details to their billing account because i told them i moved home. parents not noticing because they used to get overpayed refunds so its just part of their normality. so i spent hours and hours on phone multiple reps. its a manager actually look at it and confirmed the error and addressed it. but they wont give me a refund, and just apologize me. im never giving bank details to do automatic debit again. how hydro ottawa handle their customers data is alarming and should concern everyone.

3:40 am. 2nd rye proofing and Marisol spots it again. It's a library book, sitting on top of the flour bin by the back door. Plastic cover cold from being out in the alley. 4 Thursdays in a row. Same book. A Field Guide to Night Birds. Stamped Eastgate Branch, due 3 weeks ago. Every time she finds it she takes it to the drop box heading home. Every Thursday it comes back like the building borrowed it.

Wipes hands on apron, opens it. A folded index card falls out from the barn owls page. It's written: You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread till 5 am. I walk my mother's dog then since she cant anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I just keep not wanting to. —R.

Reads it twice while oven timer counts down. Outside the fan's on and humping warm air into the dark. She flips card. Uses the grease pencil she marks trays with, writes: Rye's out at 4:15. She tears a heel off yesterday's loaf, wraps it in wax paper, sets the book on top and props the back door open just an inch.

I used Ryanair as a poor student. My ex-partner lived in Sweden and it was the cheapest way to get there. Honestly the whole experience was awful. At the airport staff confiscated my £20 L’Occitane shower gel. Insisted it was over the liquid limit. It wasn’t. But they said I could get it back if I bought a 100ml bottle from the airport pharmacy. So I did and came back and nobody knew what I was talking about. £20 gone. I was absolutely furious. At the gate I got charged an extra £5 for having a bottle of water in my hand luggage. Bought it inside the airport and they still charged me. Ryanair stopped flying Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta so now I fly Norwegian. Their customer service is poor ironically too, but the planes feel newer, less outdated than Ryanair’s.

I am not alone here with this. Got a real soaking Tuesday and by Thursday half my Brandywines had split. I can see the seam running down the side of the fruit. Its the dry spell then a deluge story. The insides absorb water faster than the skin can stretch. The Sungolds are mostly holding up, but I have a few that look like they might go the same way. Nothing really can be done after the fact, other than getting that two day schedule more even. But it doesn't matter once the sky decided to let it all out at once. From what is left on the vines you should be able to get a fair crop. Pick the split ones and use them elsewhere. Its more of a pain with the Brandywines. That thick skin is really a liability in this type of storm. If we can not get the Sungolds taking in water so much all at once, you might have better luck.

I was reading something about the College Board and how ridiculously hypocritical they are. My friend took a subject test for the SAT, its meant to be one hour, but the proctor gave them like twenty minutes extra, and he just didn't notice. She did all the right things to maintain the integrity of the test and she reached out and reported it through the hotline. They came out and they investigated it and found that the proctor wasn't really accountable. So it turns out in their investigation that there wasn't enough evidence to really hold the proctor or other students accountable, but for my friend she was held accountable. They found that her score wasn't valid because of her misconduct and that her score was cancelled. And yet, they didn't do anything to the proctor who actually committed the error, so the one who actually committed the error wasn't held accountable, it's the one who reported it who's being punished.

Hi, just writing about that billing change. The Pro plan price moves from $12 to $15 per month on January 1st 2027. For your next invoice this will be seen. But if you're on an annual plan and have paid the 12 rate for one year, you will keep it till it renews, then it moves to 15. There's nothing you can do on your end to avoid this. If you're on monthly, you just get the new price.

There is a pricing page on your account, it will show you breakdown of all plans and where your renewal sits. On that page you'll see your next renewal date. If that date is on or after Jan 1st 2027, you move to the new price. We send a heads up a few months before renewal, so you'll have time to do something like cancel or change plans. But if you're already past renewal date or are on monthly plan, you just move to $15 and there's nothing to do.

Let me know if you have questions about how this applies to your set up, but most common questions are in the help center.

Best,
Dan

Thursdays that book shows up. And its not on the counter either, its wedged behind the flour bins by the back door, so whoever leaves it knows I wont trip over it. Always the same one. Field Guide to North American Moths, Elmwood Branch. Due date is stamped from way back when, its gone violet. But I've never once seen anyone drop it off. I'll be elbow-deep in rye dough by 2pm and at that hour i wouldn't notice a marching band. First few weeks I just left it on the shelf by the register, and by Friday morning it was gone. Then Thursday, its back. Fine. People are strange. I'm the guy who talks to my sourdough starter so I'm not judging.

Tonight there's a note, tucked at page 114, about the luna moths. It says they only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before its gone. No signature, just pencil and it was pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper and set it behind the flour bins.

So even at a comfy temp a room can feel stuffy because temperature is only part of comfort. High humidity means less moisture evaporates from skin so air feels heavy and stale. Low airflow is an issue as well. Air movement is necessary or else your carbon dioxide, odours, and heat just accumulate and don't get dispersed. Poor ventilation traps this so it feels close. You can cool the air with AC but unless it dries or moves the air around it won't improve circulation. If you open a window and put a fan or vent in motion so you feel something different.

You always hear that remote is a win win. Been mentoring five junior engineers for two years. Not actually a win for them. These people don't want tickets, docs or the meeting schedule. If anything what they want is a seat at the design arguments and to see a senior go through a nasty bug live, to get answers before small uncertainty rolls downhill. You get that for free in an office. Remote, they have to figure out when to interrupt and how to get calls setup. If the beginner cannot explain his problem yet, he can't just make it easy on himself. So we screw up our feedback process. Short note on review reads like a judgement call. Also, when people don't get answers fast enough they lose all forward momentum. I have seen this in many teams and projects. So if you pair up and sit in front of a whiteboard they move much faster. Also they can actually grab senior attention. None of this means you don't have to have flexible schedules. This works for people who can self direct. For beginners we need to physically put them near others. That's where they build context and confidence and judgment. If you just throw laptop and calendar to a newcomer, I think this is a way to weaken technical leadership down the road.

A rain gauge is really simple, its just something that takes rain that falls on the gauge and reports it in millimeters or inches in depth. So if you had a level plain of ground and it rained on it with no evaporation, no runoff or infiltration, that's what the depth indicates. So most gauges use a funnel that's a large area, that is connected to a smaller area, and the water would come in through the funnel and rise up this smaller tube. So the same volume of water is going to rise higher in this smaller tube, so you can read smaller amounts of rain easier. And the tube will be marked to account for the area difference, so the readings are still accurate. Wind is a source of error and it's quite common that you can get undercounts with wind. Also evaporation, splashing. So when it starts raining you have to do it as soon as you can.

Bought this keyboard used for $38. Popped it out of the box and it felt fair. Some dust between keys, shiny spots on the caps, but nothing worse than you'd expect from a used board.

Good part is its genuinely comfy. I type long emails at work, and my hands stop feeling as cramped as they do on my office's stupid flat keyboard. Switches feel smooth, not too heavy. And it doesn't move around on the desk.

Problems though. The spacebar clunks. It makes a noise if I hit spacebar. Not all the time, but it happened this morning during quiet office hours so you do hear it when the office is quiet. Also, the 'e' key sticks, it repeats if you type too fast. So I get "neeed" in email, it doesn't always happen but I'm more proofing. Also asked seller what switches it is. I got a reply a week later, after the board had arrived. Not great.

But at $38 I kept it. Shipping it back just didn't seem worth the effort.

Went to the buffet on a Friday about 4:30pm, no line at all, which was nice. Two people, $130, which was a lot. Felt expensive. Before going I thought it was going to be about the same price as my favorite steakhouse. I’ve paid less at the steakhouse.

I was disappointed steak wasn’t served. With the price, you’d think there would be some steak option. They had lamb, prime rib, chicken etc. stuff you can find at any other buffet in Vegas, for much less.

Seafood, had Alaska crab legs, rock crab claws. Alaskan legs I’ve seen at many buffets, but I’ve never seen rock crab claws, so they were interesting. Problem was no crackers, staff said we can get wooden mallets, but since our table was so close to the next table I didn’t want to bang on the shells, sending shrapnel over to the people next to us, so I stuck with the legs.

The Asian station wasn’t distinctive, but it was good. Reminded me of the buffet at Rampart casino. Dessert was gelato, pastries. Nothing stood out. They also have fresh juices but I didn’t try any.

It was good and I’d say if you’re curious it’s worth going once if the wait isn’t too long. But if it’s super busy and you wait a long time, I’d reconsider.

It's an old attendance register, so it's a really useful primary source to study daily life from past communities. They carefully track where students were on a day to day basis, so we can see patterns driven by farming calendar, epidemics, weather. So it's really useful. For example, if there's a sudden drop in attendance we know maybe there's an outbreak in the area, flu, or it's harvest time and the children have to help out on the farm. So that shows the very delicate balancing act between schooling and financial needs. And then consistent absence from a particular group, you can see social inequities, cultural attitudes to school and so on. However, use with caution. Because there's a very big problem there is a very big problem which is these registers aren't always consistent and can be faked. So we got to be really careful because teachers will cheat on records, they'll make their numbers up. There's always a certain pressure to get grants or to avoid being inspected by education authorities and so on. It's not necessarily a true picture of what's going on. The reasons that they were absent aren't always explained in the records. And you have to fill in the gaps, infer it from other sources. So they're a useful quantitative framework, for understanding the society. But it really needs cross-referencing to other evidence to make sure you've got the right overall picture of social structures and daily life.

Its a float valve that connects the trough to a pressurised water line. Its got a buoyant float, usually a plastic ball or block, and it rests on the water surface and attached to a lever arm. So when the cattle drink, the level drops, the float sinks and tilts the arm and it pulls the plunger or washer away from the valve seat and then water flows into the trough. As the water rises the float lifts with it. The lever then pushes the plunger back against the seat, so it gradually narrows the opening until flow stops at the set level.

Overflow commonly happens when a worn or debris fouled washer cannot seal against the seat. It also occurs when the float is punctured and water logged, so it no longer rises enough to close the valve.
